title: Fifty years since the Emergency: Thengadi and the fight for democracy
author: Editorial Desk
summary: On 25–26 June 1975 civil liberties were suspended. The movement that followed drew in people from every field.
body:
On the night of **25 June 1975**, a proclamation of Emergency was issued under Article 352 of the Constitution on the ground of "internal disturbance". Press censorship followed within days, large numbers of political opponents were detained, and fundamental rights were curtailed. The Emergency remained in force until **21 March 1977**, a period of about nineteen months. Fifty years on, it is worth asking what it meant for workers and their organisations, and what part Dattopant Thengadi, the founder of BMS, played in the movement against it.

## How the Emergency came about

The proclamation came after a political and legal crisis. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court found Prime Minister Indira Gandhi guilty of misusing government machinery in her election campaign, voided her election and barred her from contesting for six years. On 24 June the Supreme Court upheld the verdict but allowed her to remain Prime Minister pending appeal. The next night President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency, acting on the Prime Minister's advice.

During the Emergency, the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, passed in 1971, was used to detain opponents without trial. The figures given in a standard reference work are 110,806 arrests, of which 34,988 were under MISA and 75,818 under the Defence and Internal Security of India Rules. Electricity to major newspapers was cut and censorship followed. Constitutional amendments, notably the 38th and the 42nd, altered the constitutional framework, and the 38th barred judicial review of the declaration of Emergency.

## The place of labour

Trade unions were among the groups affected. The same reference work records that strikes were banned, wages were frozen and bonuses were phased out, and that a strike called in January 1976 by one central union led to the arrest of a large number of workers. In the language of the Constitution, Article 19(1)(c) gives every citizen the right to form associations or unions, and Article 19(4) allows only reasonable restrictions in the interests of sovereignty, public order or morality. A union's right to hold meetings, publish and bargain depends on those freedoms, and under the Emergency it lost much of its practical protection.

For workers the lesson is not abstract. A union that cannot meet, speak or publish cannot bargain, and a worker who cannot join one has little else to rely on. This is why labour organisations of every outlook have an interest in the survival of democratic freedoms.

## Thengadi Ji's role

According to BMS's own tribute publications and other accounts, **Dattopant Thengadi** stepped back from his responsibilities in BMS and became involved in the Lok Sangharsh Samiti, the coordinating body of the anti-Emergency movement associated with Jayaprakash Narayan. A BMS tribute booklet describes him as Secretary of the Lok Sangharsh Samiti from December 1975 to March 1977. Accounts by his associates say that he travelled the country while the police were looking for him, met leaders of different parties, and argued that resistance should be non-violent, and that peaceful mass agitation can succeed in a democracy. These accounts come from people close to him and are not independent histories, so readers should treat the details with that in mind.

The movement was organised through underground networks, and BMS's own history records that Thengadi drew on the organisational network of the Sangh family and on his experience of public life. His own belief, according to BMS publications, was that a labour organisation cannot be indifferent to the survival of democracy, since the rights of workers depend on it. That approach is consistent with the wider philosophy associated with him, which treats the interests of labour as part of the interests of the nation.

## The end of the Emergency

Elections were held from 16 to 20 March 1977. The Janata Party won 298 seats in the Lok Sabha and the Congress 154, Mrs Gandhi lost her own seat, and Morarji Desai became India's first non-Congress Prime Minister. In 1978 the **44th Amendment** added safeguards against a repeat:

- the President can proclaim an Emergency only on the written recommendation of the Cabinet, not on the Prime Minister's advice alone;
- both Houses of Parliament must approve within one month, by a special majority, and the Emergency must be renewed every six months;
- "armed rebellion" replaced "internal disturbance" as a ground; and
- one-tenth of the members of the Lok Sabha can demand a special sitting to consider revoking it, and a simple majority can end it.

## What the Emergency teaches

- Freedom of association is not a gift of the State. Where it is suspended, workers are among the first to lose their voice.
- The institutions that protect rights, such as courts, the press and legislatures, need citizens who will defend them.
- People of very different views can work together in a common cause. The movement against the Emergency brought together political workers, lawyers, journalists, students and trade unionists.
- Safeguards written into the Constitution can be tested by events, and the 44th Amendment was an attempt to learn from that test.

## How the day is remembered

In July 2024 the Government of India announced, through a gazette notification shared by the Union Home Minister on 12 July, that 25 June would be observed every year as *Samvidhan Hatya Diwas*, to remember those who suffered during the Emergency. The announcement was made in the context of a heated political debate about the Constitution, and critics, among them the civil liberties organisation PUCL, have argued that the designation serves present political purposes. Whatever one's view of the designation, the history of the period is a part of any account of Indian labour, and it is in that spirit that BMS remembers its founder's role.

## Closing

The anniversary is a reminder that the freedoms a worker uses every day, to join a union, to assemble, to publish a demand, are not guaranteed by their mere existence on paper. They have to be used, defended and handed on. That is the part of the story that matters most to a movement of workers.
